newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: A year on, Australia's economic reforms disappoint.
newsitem.headline: A year on, Australia's economic reforms disappoint.

text.p: Australia's year-old conservative government is taking things slowly, disappointing rightwing backers who had hoped the new administration would launch itself into intensive economic reforms.

When Prime Minister John Howard's Liberal-Nationals won power on March 2 last year they had spent 13 years in opposition harping at the inadequacy of the Labor government's attempts to fix the economy.

Now wielding power themselves, the conservatives have surprised with the modesty of their plans, generally implementing only limited reforms just a little beyond what Labor had done under prime ministers Bob Hawke and Paul Keating.
Moreover, the conservatives have announced few plans for more reforms in the remainder of their three-year term.
Dissatisfaction with Howard's plans emerged as early as October when Australian media baron Rupert Murdoch complained.

"If you're going to make radical changes, you'd better make them in the first year (of government)," Murdoch said then. "I think they've been slow to do that and not appearing as radical a government as I would have hoped."

Last year's Workplace Relations Act, one of the biggest reforms, gives more influence to market forces and less to unions, but various safeguards and a continued role for industrial courts ensure that the Australian wages market still has nothing like the flexibility of Britain's or New Zealand's.
"While the Workplace Relations Act has been no doubt a step in the right direction, it has been a very small step," John Stone, a former Treasury head, told Reuters.
The conservatives' current reform programme contrasts with the ambitions they held in the early 1990s, when their plans were so radical the public refused to elect them.
In the 1993 election campaign, then Liberal-National leader John Hewson said he would sell all of Telstra Corporation, the government's market-dominating telephone company.
Howard will sell just a third of Telstra and has even sugar- coated the pill by allocating A$1 billion (US$770 million) of the expected A$8 billion proceeds to an environmental fund.

In 1993, Hewson planned a much more radical, free-market wages system and wanted to introduce a value-added consumption tax so he could lower income tax rates, which economists say are so high they discourage economic activity.

But Howard's government, noting public hostility towards Hewson's plan, has barely touched the tax system and repeatedly promises not to introduce a consumption tax at least until after the next election, still two years away.
The budget is one area that has seen big changes.
Last year's election was fought under the assumption that the budget was heading into surplus -- a fiction that suited both sides because neither wanted to talk about cuts.
But within days of taking power the new government confirmed economists' estimates that the budget was in deep deficit.
The result was a historic attack on government finances.
Howard's Treasurer, Peter Costello, cut the budget by A$7 billion -- about five percent of revenue -- to put Canberra's finances within easy reach of a surplus before the election.
Unfortunately, his tax forecasts proved optimistic. He now says a second, smaller round of pruning, between A$2 billion and A$4 billion, will be needed in this year's budget, in May.
